videoIdeas.title: The Prophet's public speaking method
videoIdeas.hook: 1,400 years before anyone sold a public speaking course, the method was already written down.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your 'Slow. Clear. Three times.' post pulled 1,977 views on an actual public speaking topic, and it's one of the only posts hitting that pillar directly. Expanding the same prophetic-method angle into a full breakdown doubles down on a format that already landed and fills your most under-served pillar.
videoIdeas.script:
Slow. Clear. Repeated three times. That was the method of the best speaker who ever lived.

Anas ibn Malik narrated that when the Prophet ﷺ spoke, he would repeat a sentence three times so it was understood. When he greeted people, he greeted them three times.

Now look at how we speak. Fast, over-explained, ten points crammed into one breath because we're scared of silence.

The man who changed the world didn't rush. He said the thing. He let it land. He said it again.

If you want people to remember one line from your next talk, stop adding. Start repeating. Slow down enough that silence does half the work for you.

What's the one line you want people to leave your next talk with? Say it three times.

visuals.setting: Plain wall or bookshelf, soft natural light. Sat or stood still, calm energy, measured delivery — the pacing of your speech should demonstrate the point. Neutral modest clothing.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'Slow. Clear. Three times.' appears one word at a time with a beat of silence between each, matching your voice.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open in total silence for 1.5 seconds before you speak — a pattern interrupt against fast-cut reels
Split-screen: left side a frantic over-edited 'guru' clip, right side you sitting still
On-screen caption that counts '1... 2... 3...' as you repeat a phrase to show the method live

videoIdeas.title: There's no such thing as a 'secular job'
videoIdeas.hook: Ibn Sina, al-Biruni and Ibn al-Nafis would not understand the phrase 'secular job.'
videoIdeas.rationale: Your post with this exact line hit 1,750 views with zero comments — strong reach, no conversation. The idea clearly resonates but was under-developed. Turning it into a sharper leadership/identity piece gives people something to argue with, which drives comments you weren't getting.
videoIdeas.script:
Ibn Sina, al-Biruni, Ibn al-Nafis — none of them would understand the phrase 'secular job.'

To them there was no wall between what you believe and what you build. The physician, the astronomer, the engineer — their work was worship, not a break from it.

We built that wall much later. And most of us didn't even build it. We inherited it. We clocked in, left our deen at the door, picked it back up on Friday.

So you end up with two versions of yourself. The one at work who is 'professional.' And the one at the masjid who is 'practising.' Neither fully honest.

The people who actually led this Ummah never split themselves in half. Your work is not the opposite of your deen. It's the arena for it.

What would your job look like if you stopped treating it as separate?

visuals.setting: Film somewhere that reads 'work' — a desk, a workspace, or walking through a city in smart-casual clothing. Confident, grounded delivery.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text listing the three names 'Ibn Sina. Al-Biruni. Ibn al-Nafis.' stacking on screen as you say them, then the phrase 'secular job' appears and a line visibly strikes through it.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-walk through an office or street, as if caught mid-thought
Hold up or gesture to a laptop/notebook as the 'arena' prop on the close
On-screen punchline 'You inherited the wall. You didn't build it.' held on a still frame

videoIdeas.title: What's the last thing you upgraded in yourself?
videoIdeas.hook: New model every September. Same habits every morning.
videoIdeas.rationale: This is your highest-performing non-political post by engagement quality — 4,673 views, 168 likes, and it's pure mindset in your voice. It's proof your audience will reward reflective content when the hook is tight. Running it back with a sharper CTA should lift the comment count, which was only 7 despite a direct question.
videoIdeas.script:
New model every September. Same habits every morning.

The phone in your hand has been upgraded four times. You? Same sleep, same scroll, same excuses.

Technology moves forward on its own. A new chip, a new camera, you don't have to do anything. It just arrives.

People don't work like that. Nobody gets upgraded automatically. You have to be formed — slowly, deliberately, one habit at a time. And that part is uncomfortable, so most people skip it and buy the phone instead.

The upgrade you actually need isn't on sale in September. It's the thing you've been avoiding all year.

So — what's the last thing you genuinely upgraded in yourself? Not your phone. You. Drop it below.

visuals.setting: Clean, minimal room or at a desk, morning light. Calm but direct. Could hold a phone as a prop then set it down.
visuals.visualHook: Hold up your phone to camera, then on-screen text 'Upgraded 4 times' over the phone, cutting to text 'You: 0' over your face.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open setting a phone face-down on a table as the first action
On-screen text punchline 'The upgrade isn't on sale in September'
Quick cut montage implied by text: 'New model. Same habits.' as a two-card contrast

videoIdeas.title: Save this before your 20s run out
videoIdeas.hook: If you're a young Muslim in your 20s, save this now — because nobody's going to say this to your face.
videoIdeas.rationale: doctordaanish's '20s' saveable listicle pulled 92k views and 5,530 likes — the save-driven advice format is working hard in this niche right now and you have nothing in it. A blunt, non-fluffy version aimed specifically at young Muslims is a clear gap and plays to your 'sharp older brother' voice.
videoIdeas.script:
If you're a young Muslim in your 20s, save this. Because nobody's going to say this to your face.

One. Stop waiting to 'feel ready' to practise properly. Readiness isn't coming. You start weak and you build.

Two. Your circle is quietly deciding your next ten years. Pick people who pray, who read, who build — or inherit their habits by accident.

Three. The money will come and go. The character you build now is the only thing you actually keep.

Four. Learn to speak. Being right in your head is worthless if you freeze the second people look at you.

And five. Stop performing your deen online and neglecting it in private. One of those is real. The other is a costume.

Save it. Read it again in a week. Then actually do one of them.

visuals.setting: Direct to camera, close framing, confident and slightly intense 'listen to me' energy. Plain background so the on-screen text carries weight.
visuals.visualHook: Big bold on-screen text 'SAVE THIS' with a numbered list building (1–5) down the side as you speak, so viewers see there's a payoff to staying.
otherHookIdeas: Point directly at the camera on 'nobody's going to say this to your face'
On-screen save-icon animation nudging the gesture early
End card freezing all 5 points on screen so people pause to save

videoIdeas.title: Young Muslims are building third spaces — stop mocking them
videoIdeas.hook: Young British Muslims are quietly building something, and the loudest people online can only sneer at it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your third-spaces post did 1,856 views but only 3 comments — a leadership/community topic that under-converted. It sits between your viral political reach and your quieter mindset content. Framing it as a defence of builders vs critics taps the confrontational energy that drives your biggest posts while staying on the leadership pillar.
videoIdeas.script:
Young British Muslims are building something. Cafés. Community hubs. Study circles. Spaces where people can actually meet, learn and belong.

And the loudest people online? All they can do is sneer. 'Not Islamic enough.' 'Just a vibe.' 'Where's the real work.'

It's always the same. The people doing nothing have the strongest opinions about the people doing something.

Building a space where a lonely brother or sister feels they belong is not a lesser work. For a lot of people that room is the first reason they come back at all.

Leadership isn't a caption criticising the builders. It's being one. It's opening the door, filling the room, and carrying the cost when it's quiet.

So before you critique the next third space — what have you actually built?

visuals.setting: Film in or outside a café / community space if possible, or walking through one. Warmer, lived-in environment. Slightly fired-up but controlled delivery.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a real third space — people sat talking, a café counter — with on-screen text 'They built this. The internet mocked it.'
otherHookIdeas: Cold open walking into a busy community room mid-sentence
On-screen contrast text: 'Critics: 0 built. Builders: 1 room full.'
End on a direct challenge caption frozen on screen: 'What have you built?'

videoIdeas.title: You don't have an opinion, you have a repost
videoIdeas.hook: Half of you don't actually have opinions. You have reposts.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your political posts prove you get the most reach when you're blunt and confrontational (8,613 and 8,579 views). lifeofdinoo_ went viral calling out irresponsible online content. This takes that same call-out energy but points it at a mindset/character problem instead of a single news event — broader shelf life, same edge.
videoIdeas.script:
Half of you don't have opinions. You have reposts.

Something happens in the Ummah, and within an hour your story is full of the same three infographics everyone else shared. Same wording. Same outrage. Same nothing.

And it feels like doing something. It isn't. It's borrowing a thought, wearing it for 24 hours, and letting it disappear.

An opinion costs you. You had to read, think, and risk being wrong. A repost costs you a tap.

I'm not saying stop sharing. I'm saying know the difference between amplifying a cause and performing one.

Next time before you repost — ask if you could explain it, out loud, to someone who disagreed. If you can't, you don't hold the view. You're just holding the phone.

visuals.setting: Close, direct to camera, plain background. Sharp, unbothered tone — not shouting, just certain. Phone in hand as a prop.
visuals.visualHook: Hold phone up showing a 'reposted to story' animation, then on-screen text 'This isn't an opinion.'
otherHookIdeas: Cold open tapping 'share' on a story then looking up at the camera flatly
On-screen punchline 'A repost costs a tap. An opinion costs you.'
Pattern interrupt: lock the phone and set it down on 'you're just holding the phone'

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your biggest post at 8,613 views — the hook names a concrete historical grievance (Iraq, Afghanistan) and connects it to a live threat (Iran), which is exactly the blunt, current-affairs framing that pushes your reach beyond your 1,322 followers.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 75 likes and 24 comments on 8,613 views is a weak conversion — this reached a lot of non-followers who didn't connect to you as a person. Add a clear through-line to who YOU are (leadership/mindset angle) or a pinned comment that gives people a reason to follow, so viral reach turns into follows instead of a one-off view spike.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your best like-to-view ratio on a political post — 208 likes on 8,579 views. The 'can't believe we're still discussing this in 2026' hook is confident and dismissive in your voice, and people rewarded the stance.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: The caption is cut off mid-sentence ('feel bett...') and comments are low at 12. Finish the thought and end on a direct question or a line people want to argue with. A strong stance like this should be provoking far more than 12 comments at this reach.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your strongest non-political post — 4,673 views, 168 likes — and it's pure mindset in your signature short-line style ('New model every September. Same habits every morning.'). This proves your audience will reward reflective content when the hook is this tight. Lean into this format.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 7 comments despite ending on a direct question ('What's the last thing you upgraded in yourself?'). The question is good but generic enough to scroll past. Make the CTA harder to ignore — force a binary or a confession ('Name one. Not your phone.') so answering feels specific.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 2,786 views and 123 likes on a personal, humanising post — 'might not be the fastest, but I'm in the room' is quotable and shows a side of you beyond commentary. This builds the parasocial trust that converts viewers into followers.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's floating as a standalone running post with no tie to your pillars. The 'in the room' line is a ready-made mindset/leadership lesson — spell that out in the caption or a second line so the post does double duty instead of reading as a personal fitness update.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is one of your only posts squarely on the public speaking pillar, and the hook 'Slow. Clear. Three times.' is excellent — punchy, prophetic, and specific. 1,977 views shows the topic has legs and you should be making far more of it.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 3 comments and the reach is lower than your political posts, which suggests the visual hook didn't stop the scroll as hard as the written one. Give the first 3 seconds an on-screen text or silence-based pattern interrupt that demonstrates the 'slow' method visually, and push this pillar more often since it's your biggest content gap.
